implementation_notes: Kotlin has three scope-bound forms and no need for a guard class: synchronized(lock) { ... } (a stdlib inline function over the JVM monitor, released on every exit path), lock.withLock { ... } from kotlin.concurrent for java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock (acquire, run the block, unlock in a finally inside the inline function) and kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex.withLock { ... } for suspending code, which holds the lock across suspension points without blocking a thread. Choose by execution model: plain threads use synchronized or withLock, coroutines use the suspending Mutex, and mixing the two is a bug.
pitfalls: synchronized() blocks the carrier thread; inside a coroutine it can stall the whole dispatcher - use a suspending Mutex for suspending critical sections.
kotlinx.coroutines Mutex is not reentrant: acquiring it inside its own withLock suspends forever.
withLock is inline, so a non-local return out of the block needs the right label (return@withLock vs return) or the released scope differs from what the reader assumes.
Holding a coroutine Mutex across an indefinite suspension (network, user input) turns mutual exclusion into an application-level deadlock.
Lock.withLock unlocks in a finally, but the Lock itself is still a JVM lock: unlocking from a different thread is illegal, and a coroutine that hops threads must not hold it.
